summary: Chapter 103 has 15 verses in the Charles text. Enoch swears by the Great and Honoured Mighty One, claims he has read heavenly tablets and holy books where goodness, joy and glory are prepared for the righteous dead, then answers the righteous lament — 'We have toiled laboriously, became the tail, dominion over us hated and smote us, no place to flee, rulers did not attend but concealed oppression' — and threatens sinners with darkness, chains and burning flame.
whyItMatters: It preserves both complaint and ledger: a litany of being made few, devoured and ignored, answered by tablets that record joy for the dead righteous and grievous judgment for their oppressors.

context.author: Pseudonymously attributed to Enoch; modern scholarship sees distinct booklets composed in Aramaic and later rendered through Greek into Ge'ez
context.audience: Jewish readers under Hellenistic pressure and later the Ethiopian Orthodox Church that preserves the complete Ge'ez book
context.date: Booklets from the third century BC to the first century AD; the Ge'ez collection preserved from late antiquity and copied from the fifteenth century onward
context.setting: From Mount Hermon and the wilderness to the heavenly throne room and the chambers of the luminaries, narrated as Enoch's tours and dreams
context.literaryForm: Epistle — hortatory address, woe-oracle and blessing for the righteous in the last days

outline.heading: Tablets of joy
outline.note: Verses 1-4 swear by the Great One, claiming heavenly tablets where joy is written for righteous spirits.

outline.heading: Woe in wealth and Sheol
outline.note: Verses 5-8 pronounce woe on sinners dying in wealth whose souls descend to Sheol.

outline.heading: Lament of the righteous
outline.note: Verses 9-12 quote lament: 'We toiled, became tail, dominion hated us, no helper'.

outline.heading: No place to flee, rulers conceal
outline.note: Verses 13-15 close finding no place to flee while rulers helped robbers and concealed oppression.

keyVerses.text: Now, therefore, I swear to you, the righteous, by the glory of the Great and Honoured and
keyVerses.why: This opening verse establishes the chapter's setting — speaker, hearers, and the charge or woe that governs what follows.

keyVerses.text: And into darkness and chains and a burning flame where there is grievous judgement shall your spirits enter; And the great judgement shall be for all the generations of the world. Woe to you, for ye shall have no peace.
keyVerses.why: This middle verse carries the central turn — whether verdict, wonder, or reversal — distilling the chapter's main claim.

keyVerses.text: And they helped those who robbed us and devoured us and those who made us few; and they concealed their oppression, and they did not remove from us the yoke of those that devoured us and dispersed us and murdered us, and they concealed their murder, and remembered not that they had lifted up their hands against us.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse seals the chapter's movement and shows where exhortation, woe, or promise finally lands.

questions.question: What is actually happening in 1 Enoch 103, and who is speaking or being shown something?
questions.answer: In this chapter the seer Enoch is shown a further stage of the visions that began in chapter 37. The voice or angelic guide presents a specific judgment or heavenly order, and Enoch records what is said and seen so it can be transmitted. The chapter's 15 verses move from announcement to its content and then to its effect on those who hear it.

questions.question: What key title or image appears here — for example Head of Days, Lord of Spirits, or Son of Man / Elect One — and how does Charles render it?
questions.answer: Charles keeps the book's distinctive titles — Head of Days for the enthroned Ancient One and Elect One or Son of Man for the heavenly assessor — with initial capitals so the repetition is visible. In this chapter the title signals which courtroom participant is speaking or being enthroned, not merely a poetic flourish, and the briefing explains that the three names for the assessor describe one office.

questions.question: Why does the chapter link the fate of 'kings and the mighty' to a throne or judgment?
questions.answer: Parables and Epistle passages repeatedly stage a reversal: those who felt secure on earth — kings, the exalted, those who dwell on the earth — are summoned before the Head of Days and the Elect One. The judgment is not a private opinion but a courtroom scene with a throne, and the verdict exposes that earthly power does not survive the heavenly audit.

questions.question: How does this chapter compare to Daniel 7 or Genesis 6, which share throne and Watcher material?
questions.answer: Daniel 7 supplies the throne and Ancient of Days / son-of-man background that the Parables reuses with its Head of Days and Son of Man, while Genesis 6:1-4 supplies the sons-of-God entry point that the Watcher story expands. This chapter should be read alongside those passages as reuse, not proof — a cross-reference is a route for comparison, not evidence that two texts mean the same thing.

questions.question: What does the chapter expect from its readers — warning, comfort, or instruction about time?
questions.answer: Like other Enoch booklets, the chapter ends not with curiosity alone but with a stance for the righteous: trust that the judgment is certain, refrain from the Watchers' transgression, and keep the revealed instruction. Even calendrical or astronomical details aim at practice — counting days faithfully and preserving the book for children — rather than speculation.

questions.question: A hard verse: does this chapter teach that God 'repented' or that angels literally hold scourges and chains?
questions.answer: In 55:1 the Head of Days 'repented' translates a Semitic idiom for a decisive turn, not that God learns something new, and in chapters like 56 the angels of punishment with scourges and chains are courtroom imagery for assured execution of sentence. Readers differ on how literally to picture such agents, but the text's point is certainty of judgment, not a material description of heavenly ironwork.

questions.question: Where does the Charles English show its editorial marks — ⌈⌉ or [ ] — and why are they kept?
questions.answer: Charles uses ⌈⌉ for conjectured readings and [ ] for words he supplies to make sense of the Ge'ez, and the hosted text preserves them verbatim. They signal where the Ge'ez–Greek chain is thin, inviting caution rather than filling the gap with a confident paraphrase. The book briefing's textual history explains that no complete Hebrew original survives.

questions.question: How does this small unit connect to the larger anthology — Watchers, Parables, Luminaries, Dream Visions, or Epistle?
questions.answer: Chapters 91–108 belong to the Epistle and its appendices — weeks, woes, exhortation, Noah's birth, and final blessing — completing the anthology's arc from Watcher descent to calendar, animal allegory, and finally direct address to the righteous about wealth, patience, and books.

glossary.def: What Enoch says he has read where goodness, joy and glory are prepared for spirits of those who have died in righteousness (103:2).
Title in the oath 'by the glory of the Great and Honoured and Mighty One in dominion' that opens chapter 103.
